introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et mention manuscrite d'adresse web ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les effectifs sont donnés en ordres de grandeur prudents (« roughly nine to ten million », « about two million »).

Question 2 : l'énoncé imprimé associe « the Jihad in Futa Jallon » aux dates 1854-1864. Ces dates correspondent à la guerre sainte d'Al-Hajj Umar Tall (empire toucouleur, parti de Dinguiraye, en bordure du Fouta-Djalon), alors que le jihad du Fouta-Djalon proprement dit date d'environ 1725 (Karamoko Alfa). Le sujet est recopié tel quel ; le corrigé signale la divergence et traite le mouvement de 1854-1864, avec le jihad du Fouta-Djalon en arrière-plan. L'année de début de la guerre sainte d'Umar est donnée de façon prudente (1852 ou 1854 selon les sources).

Question 2 : détails à vérifier par un historien (siège de Médine en 1857, prise de Ségou en 1861 et de Hamdallahi en 1862, mort d'Umar en 1864, chute de Ségou face à Archinard en 1890) ; ils sont cités conformément à l'historiographie courante, mais le corrigé ne s'appuie pas sur des chiffres.

Question 7 : les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, invitation des « Immortal Seven » et acquittement des sept évêques le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre) ; le corrigé précise le choix du calendrier julien.
Question 4 : le massacre de Thiaroye (décembre 1944), les émeutes d'Accra (1948) et la conférence de Brazzaville (1944) sont cités sans bilan chiffré, le nombre exact de victimes étant discuté.

Question 5 : exemples de coups d'État (Togo 1963, Ghana 1966, Nigeria 1966, Ouganda 1971, Éthiopie 1974, Mali 2020) cités sans chiffres ; la formule « very many people were killed » remplace volontairement tout bilan sous Amin, très discuté.

Question 12 : la liste des suspensions et départs (Nigeria 1995, Fidji, Zimbabwe 2003, Gambie 2013 puis retour 2018) et l'adhésion du Cameroun en 1995 sont citées de mémoire historique ; aucun chiffre financier n'est avancé.

Questions à thème régional : les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `military coups in africa`, `refugee crisis in africa`, `league of nations`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à reverifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Assess the relative importance of the birth of the Prince of Wales to the outbreak of the Glorious Revolution of 1688.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Glorious Revolution of 1688-89 was the removal of the Catholic king James II of England by an invasion led by his Protestant son-in-law and nephew, William of Orange, with the support of leading English politicians. The birth of a son to James II and Mary of Modena on 10 June 1688 (Old Style dates are used here) created a Catholic male heir. The question requires an assessment of how important that birth was compared with the other causes of the revolution. The birth was a decisive *trigger*, but the underlying causes, above all James's religious and political policies, were more important.

**1. The importance of the birth.**
- Before June 1688 the heirs to the throne were James's two Protestant daughters, Mary (married to William of Orange) and Anne. Many Protestants tolerated James's Catholic rule as temporary, expecting a Protestant succession.
- The birth of James Francis Edward replaced this prospect with the likelihood of a permanent Catholic dynasty, since a son took precedence over the daughters. Opposition now saw no chance of waiting for a change.
- The birth led to rumours that the baby was a substitute smuggled into the queen's bed in a warming pan, showing the extent of distrust of the king.
- It gave William and his allies urgency and a justification for action: it ended the hope of a peaceful solution and led the opposition to act. On 30 June 1688, the day of the acquittal of the Seven Bishops, the "Immortal Seven" (a group of English noblemen and politicians) sent an invitation to William to come with an army.

**2. Other and deeper causes.**
- *Religion.* James II was an openly Catholic king in a Protestant country with a long fear of "popery". He appointed Catholics to the army, the government, the universities and the Church (for example the Magdalen College affair of 1687) and set up the Ecclesiastical Commission in 1686 to discipline the Church of England. The revocation of the Edict of Nantes in France (1685) strengthened fears of Catholic persecution.
- *Use of royal power.* James used the dispensing power to exempt Catholics from the Test Acts (confirmed by the court in the case of Godden v Hales, 1686), issued Declarations of Indulgence in 1687 and 1688 and ordered the clergy to read the second Declaration, which led to the trial of the Seven Bishops. He dissolved Parliament, tried to pack a new one, and built a standing army, which alarmed those who remembered Charles I and the Civil War.
- *The alienation of the Tories and the Church of England.* The Tory gentry and Anglican clergy, traditionally loyal to the Crown, were driven into opposition by attacks on the Church, and the acquittal of the Seven Bishops on 30 June showed how widespread opposition was.
- *The Dutch dimension.* William of Orange was already preparing an expedition in 1688. For William, the English crown was important for his struggle against Louis XIV's France: England would join the anti-French alliance. He was also married to the Protestant heir, Mary. The birth of a Catholic son threatened to remove his wife's claim and the prospects of an Anglo-Dutch alliance.
- *The invasion and its success.* William landed at Torbay on 5 November 1688. The army and the nobility deserted James; James fled in December and eventually left the country, and in 1689 Parliament (the Convention) declared the throne vacant and offered it to William and Mary, who accepted the Declaration (later Bill) of Rights.

**3. Assessment.** The birth was not the cause of the revolution: James had already alienated the political nation and William had been preparing intervention. However, it altered the political calculations at a decisive moment, turning discontent into rebellion, and it explains the timing and the speed of the invitation. Without the birth, many people might have waited for James's death and a Protestant successor. Without James's policies, however, the birth would not have mattered.

**Conclusion.** The birth of the Prince of Wales was an important catalyst or immediate cause, but it was less important than the long-term causes: James II's Catholicism, his use of royal prerogative, his attacks on the Anglican Church and Parliament, and the opposition of William. The birth turned a dissatisfaction that could have been endured into a revolution that was considered necessary.
